b: Enterprise software evaluation is the structured process organizations use to compare, score, and select software against business, technical, and financial requirements. According to Forrester’s 2026 State of Business Buying, the average B2B buying group now includes 13 stakeholders spanning nearly every department, and nine external influencers. That complexity, combined with the lack of a shared process, is why so many evaluations stall.

This guide gives enterprise buyers that process. Revenue stakeholders will walk away with a scorecard framework, demo script, pilot plan, TCO model, reference-call script, and a stakeholder alignment approach that can be put to use on your team’s next evaluation no matter how many vendors you’re comparing.

How to Make Your Final Decision With Confidence

Enterprise software evaluation is a structured process for selecting software against business, technical, and financial requirements. Whether it’s a CRM, an ERP system, or a content management platform, the evaluation muscle is the same.
Done well, it’s a cross-functional exercise that determines whether an organization gets significant value from a platform or ends up with another underused line item.

A weighted evaluation is important because feature comparisons alone rarely predict success. Zylo’s 2024 SaaS Management Report found that 51% of large enterprise software licenses go unused. This gap usually traces back to evaluations that scored features instead of fit. Software that seemingly meets every requirement on a checklist can still fail to be adopted, integrate with the systems teams already rely on, or unify data across departments that need a shared view of the customer.

The stronger predictor of outcomes is alignment. Does the software fit how people actually work? Does it connect to the rest of the stack without heavy lift? And is the data it generates usable by every team that needs it, not just the team that bought it? These factors are why enterprise software evaluation works best as a cross-functional go-to-market alignment rather than a procurement checkbox owned by one department and approved by the rest.
Enterprise Software Evaluation Criteria You Can Score Today
Score every vendor against these seven questions, and revenue stakeholders will have a defensible, comparable basis for the software shortlist, regardless of category.
What business outcomes must the software prove?
Any product that isn’t going to move the needle for the business is a non-starter, says Philip Huthwaite, CEO at 5app.

“Every time I’m procuring new software, the vendor has to be able to share concrete business impact numbers with me,” Huthwaite states. “I don’t just want to know about activity; I want to know if your product will increase my sales or help me attract more leads or reduce support tickets.”
Before looking at any features, define the outcome the software needs to produce. This could be:
Write it down as a number with a timeframe attached. Vendors should be able to speak not only to whether the feature exists, but also to how comparable customers achieved that outcome.
“Case studies or customer success statistics are a great way to convince me,” adds Huthwaite. “I will always choose a vendor who can prove business impact over one who can’t.”
Pro tip: Ask each vendor to map their product directly to your stated outcome in the first call. If they can’t, that indicates the fit conversation is starting with features rather than results.
How will users adopt and work daily?

The best-scoring software on paper isn’t useful if the people who are supposed to use it daily don’t find it usable. Evaluate the actual workflow by considering how many clicks it takes to complete a core task, how much retraining existing staff will need, and whether the interface matches how your teams already think about their work.
Can it integrate and govern data end-to-end?

Enterprise software rarely lives in isolation. It needs to integrate data cleanly to and from your CRM, marketing automation, ERP, and data warehouse without manual exports or brittle point-to-point connections. This is also where data governance requirements enter the evaluation. There must be governance over who can see what data, how sensitive fields are handled, and how the vendor supports compliance requirements such as data residency and retention.

What we like: Platforms that treat integration and governance as core product capabilities tend to hold up better as organizations scale. For example, HubSpot’s Sensitive Data, available on Enterprise subscriptions, lets teams mark properties in HubSpot Smart CRM as sensitive, add application-layer encryption, and limit who can view or edit them with field-level permissions, which is the kind of governance capability worth asking every vendor about.
Is security and compliance baked in?

Security and compliance can’t be a follow-up question after you’ve already picked a favorite vendor. Ask for SOC 2 reports, data processing agreements, and uptime history upfront. Vendors serious about enterprise buyers typically maintain a dedicated trust resource. HubSpot’s Trust Center is a useful example of what to expect. Security certifications, compliance documentation, and status history are all in one place, rather than scattered across sales decks.

Also confirm the basics that enterprise IT teams expect by default, including single sign-on support and granular, role-based permissions. At scale, these are usually deal-breakers if missing. Single Sign-On and User Permissions are the kind of controls every enterprise evaluator must confirm in writing. Don’t assume a vendor offers security features unless you’ve asked them about it.
Will it scale with your roadmap?

Look beyond where your organization is today and score software against where it will be in two to three years. That means asking about API rate limits, record and seat ceilings, and how pricing changes as usage grows. Left unchecked, these elements become hidden costs later.

Even at the enterprise level, software is a relationship. Evaluate response times on support tickets, the strength of the onboarding team, and whether the vendor has a track record with organizations of your size and complexity.

AI readiness now belongs on every enterprise scorecard. Ask whether AI features are native to the platform or bolted on, whether they’re trained on your organization’s data or a generic model, and whether the vendor has a clear roadmap for how AI capabilities will expand. For example, AI Guided Selling shows what it looks like when AI is built to directly improve rep productivity rather than added as a marketing checkbox.
How to Align Stakeholders and KPIs Before You Start

Stakeholder alignment requires input from IT, security, finance, procurement, marketing, sales, service, and operations teams. Misalignment is the single biggest reason evaluations stall. Research on software project failures consistently points to conflicting goals and inconsistent requirements as leading causes of delay and abandonment, well ahead of any issue with the software itself.
Yad Senapathy, founder and CEO of Project Management Training Institute (PMTI), experienced firsthand how misalignment can impact the entire evaluation process.

“I worked with a client a few years ago where the software evaluation lasted for four months without reaching a conclusion,” recalls Senapathy. “IT wanted one thing, the finance department wanted something entirely different, while end users had not even been consulted on their needs. This situation cannot be called a software issue but instead a scope issue.”
Senapathy recommends creating a brief agreement document for all stakeholders to sign before ever meeting with a vendor.

“This document should involve the business department, IT department, project managers and end-users,” he says. “It outlines what success should look like within ninety days, what number will demonstrate success, and what person will be responsible for this number in the case of failure.”
Use this checklist to get stakeholders aligned before vendor calls:
Name the decision-maker. Committees evaluate together, but a single individual makes the final call. Identify that person before the evaluation and shortlisting even starts.

Agree on success metrics up front. Every stakeholder should be able to state, in one sentence, what “success” looks like, and it should be tied to a business KPI. If finance and sales define success differently, that gap will resurface at contract time.

Map who needs to sign off and when. Security review, legal review, and procurement each have their own timeline. Build them into your evaluation calendar instead of discovering them after you’ve already picked a vendor.
Document requirements before demos, not during them. Requirements gathered during a live demo tend to reflect whatever the vendor just showed, not what the business actually needs.
Building the Shortlist and Selection Process

The evaluation process follows scope, shortlist, demo, pilot, TCO analysis, reference calls, and final selection. Building the shortlist is where your requirements and scorecard turn into a manageable set of candidates, typically three to five vendors.
What to Include in Your RFI or RFP
Keep your RFI or RFP focused on what actually differentiates vendors for your use case.
Business outcomes the software must support, with your defined success metrics attached.
Required integrations, listed by name, including your CRM, ERP system, or data warehouse, rather than as a generic "integrations" line.
Security and compliance requirements, including SSO, permissions, and data residency.
Implementation timeline expectations and what support is included.
Pricing structure, including how costs change as usage scales.
Avoid generic feature checklists as they produce generic answers. A vendor’s response to specific, business-tied requirements tells you far more than a checked box on a 200-line feature matrix.
How to Build a Balanced Scoring Matrix

A software evaluation scorecard compares vendors with weighted criteria and documented evidence. Build yours around the seven criteria above, weighted by what matters most to your organization. For example, a highly regulated industry might weight security at 30%, while a fast-scaling team might weight adoption and time-to-value higher.

For each vendor, score every criterion 1-5 and require a note on why, with a link to documentation, a demo timestamp, or a reference quote. Scores without evidence tend to drift toward whoever gave the best presentation rather than toward whoever’s product actually fits.
Running Demos and Pilots That Inform Teams
Software demos should use role-based scripts tied to real workflows and acceptance criteria.
Demo Script You Can Copy And Customize
Send this structure to vendors ahead of time so the demo is built around your workflows.
Open with your top business outcome. Ask the vendor to show, specifically, how their product moves that metric.
Walk through one real workflow, end to end. Use an actual scenario your team handles weekly. This is more valuable than a generic use case.
Test the integration you care about most. Ask to see the connection to your CRM or core system live, rather than just described on a slide.
Have an actual end user drive part of the demo. If someone from your team can navigate the interface with minimal guidance during the demo, that’s a strong sign that adoption may be successful.
Ask what breaks at scale. Push the vendor to describe a limitation instead of focusing on its strengths. Every product has one, and vendors willing to name theirs are usually more trustworthy.
Pilot Success Criteria and No-Go Signals

Pilot success criteria should be defined before the pilot starts. Set specific, measurable thresholds such as adoption rate among pilot users, time to complete a core task, or data integration and accuracy after sync, and agree on them with stakeholders in advance.

Watch for no-go signals during the pilot itself. This could be support tickets that go unanswered for days, integration issues that require workarounds rather than fixes, or pilot users reverting to their old tools without being asked. Any one of these late in a pilot is a preview of what post-launch support will look like at full scale.

Sandbox environments make pilots lower-risk. Testing configurations and integrations before committing production data is standard practice for serious enterprise evaluations. HubSpot’s Sandbox tools are built for exactly this kind of pre-go-live testing.

Enterprise software connects to dozens of other systems, including CRM, ERP, data warehouse, and marketing automation. Evaluating integration depth up front prevents the “integration sprawl” that inflates both cost and risk after go-live. A unified customer platform can reduce integration sprawl, data silos, and adoption friction compared to stitching together point solutions after the fact.
Documented, versioned API access and not just a support-ticket-based integration process.
Real-time or near-real-time event/webhook support, if your use case requires it.
Clear rate limits and what happens (and what it costs) when you exceed them.
Native connectors to your core systems, versus custom-build-required integrations.
A data model your teams can actually map to existing records without a full re-architecture.
For gaps a native connector doesn’t cover, an iPaaS platform is often the more sustainable fix than a one-off custom build.

Data quality also belongs in this conversation. Evaluation teams should ask how a vendor handles duplicate records, incomplete fields, and ongoing data enrichment. HubSpot’s Data Quality Software and Data Enrichment tools serve as useful reference points for what “data readiness” should look like on a modern platform.

Choosing Between Cloud, On-Prem, and Hybrid

The deployment model is one of the earliest decisions that shapes everything downstream, including cost, security posture, and how fast you can scale. Here’s how to decide which one makes the most sense for your organization.

A cloud platform makes sense for most organizations today, particularly where IT teams want to avoid owning infrastructure and where scalability needs are hard to predict. It shifts security and disaster recovery investment to the vendor, but it also means accepting vendor-managed update cycles and, in some cases, less control over exactly where data lives.

On-premise still fits organizations with strict regulatory requirements around data residency, or those with existing infrastructure investment they need to protect. It comes with a higher upfront cost and requires internal IT resources for ongoing maintenance and upgrades, but it offers the most direct control over data and security configuration.

A hybrid deployment is increasingly common for organizations that need to keep sensitive data on-premises while still leveraging cloud scalability for less sensitive workloads. It’s the more operationally complex option, but it’s often the right answer for regulated industries that can’t fully commit to either extreme. This often includes financial services, healthcare, and government organizations.

Best for: Fast-scaling teams without heavy regulatory constraints generally get the most value from cloud deployment. Heavily regulated industries with strict data residency rules are usually better served by hybrid or on-premises, at least for the systems of record.
Driving Adoption After You’ve Made Your Selection
Adoption risk is another criterion that should be scored during the evaluation process.

“People tend to lose interest in the technology after they have seen it for a few weeks, as soon as their initial enthusiasm is over,” says Senapthy. “They will go back to using the old spreadsheet, as it is more convenient for them, although it may cause problems for the organization.”

Build adoption into your vendor scorecard directly. Ask about onboarding structure, availability of a dedicated customer success contact, and what training resources are included versus billed separately.
Before go-live, put these in place:
A named internal champion for each affected team, identified before rollout. This individual should not be recruited after adoption stalls.
A documented, role-specific training plan that goes beyond a single generic onboarding session.
A 30/60/90-day check-in cadence with clear adoption metrics attached.
A feedback loop for early users to flag friction before it becomes a reason to revert to old tools.
Senapathy emphasizes the importance of establishing a regular check-in cadence.

“If there is no increase in usage in a team, I do not just send another reminder and label it as a training problem,” he says. “I need to understand if the system meets the requirements of the team. Ignoring this point may lead to the same problem appearing in a few months’ time.”
The goal is protecting the investment you just made the business case for. Software that scored well in evaluation but gets poor adoption produces the same outcome as choosing the wrong vendor.
Evaluating the Vendor, Not Just the Software

Choosing enterprise software means evaluating the vendor relationship, support model, and long-term viability. A product can score well on every technical criterion and still be a poor choice if the vendor is unresponsive, financially unstable, or misaligned on how the partnership should work as your needs change.
These questions are designed to surface what a sales deck won’t. Use them on every reference call:
“What did the implementation actually take, versus what you were told it would take?”
“What’s one thing you wish you’d asked the vendor before signing?”
“How has support responded when something broke or didn’t work as expected?”
“Has pricing changed since you signed, and how did the vendor handle that conversation?”
“If you were starting the evaluation over today, would you choose this vendor again?”
A vendor who offers a reference willing to answer all five candidly is showing more confidence than any demo can convey.

How to Make Your Final Decision With Confidence

A strong enterprise software evaluation is about building a process that surfaces the right evidence: business outcomes, adoption reality, integration depth, true cost, and vendor reliability. Score against defined criteria, align your stakeholders before you start, pilot before you commit at scale, and model your TCO honestly. Do that, and the final decision becomes a formality rather than a leap of faith.

Platforms built around a single, connected data model, like HubSpot Smart CRM, are worth evaluating against this framework specifically because they’re designed to reduce the integration and governance burden this guide walks through, rather than adding to it. For enterprise teams with more complex requirements around permissions, hierarchy, and governance, the Enterprise CRM edition is built to meet the exact criteria outlined above: custom objects, advanced permissions, and governance controls suited to complex organizations.

Whichever platform you land on, the framework matters more than any single vendor. Apply it consistently, and your next evaluation, regardless of category, will be faster, better documented, and far less likely to end up as another underused license a year from now.
